chunks: What is a system on chip. The question: What is a SoC?
A system on chip (SoC) is one piece of silicon that holds most of a small computer: a processor, memory, and the circuits that talk to the outside world.
Putting it all on one chip makes a product smaller and often cheaper at large volumes, and it can save power.
A few parts, such as the big main memory and the power supply, usually stay outside.
Picture an old town where each shop sits in its own village, joined by long, slow highways. A SoC is one compact city where the same shops sit a few blocks apart on short streets.
Every building has a street number, so anyone can reach it by number. The picture breaks down in one place: a chip has a fixed size and cannot hold everything.
Masters (blocks that start transactions) and slaves (blocks that respond) meet at the interconnect.
Because everything shares one address map, software talks to hardware by loads and stores. Clocking, power, reset and debug (not drawn) touch every block.
Die: the single small square of silicon that the circuits are built on. Processor core: the part that runs program instructions.
Peripheral: a block that talks to the outside world, such as a serial port (a link that sends data one bit at a time) or USB.
Interconnect: the on-chip wiring and switching that lets blocks send data to each other.
Address map: the list of numbers that says where each block lives, so software reaches a block by its number.
Microcontroller: a small SoC with a processor, built-in memory and peripherals.
The old way uses three chips: a processor, a memory chip and a serial-port chip, wired together on a board. A SoC puts all three blocks on one die.
To send a byte, the program writes it to the serial block's address. The interconnect routes that write to the serial block, which sends the byte out.
You still add a crystal (a part that sets the clock beat) outside. That is the whole idea.

"A SoC integrates a whole system, CPU cores, memory controllers, often a GPU and accelerators, peripherals like UART, SPI, USB and PCIe, plus clocks, power management and security, onto a single die, tied together by an on-chip interconnect and a shared address map.
It cuts size, power and board cost at volume, though you still need DRAM, regulators and a crystal outside, and the design effort is large. A microcontroller is a small SoC."
